claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
The starting alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and undergoes brittle failure.
Dislocations pile up at internal lamellar boundaries in the untreated alloy.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries produce local stress concentrations.
Local stress concentrations at the internal boundaries initiate microcracks and contribute to catastrophic brittle failure.
A controlled annealing treatment can promote beneficial solute segregation at internal phase boundaries.
The annealing treatment will produce solute-decorated internal interfaces.
Solute segregation will modify the chemical and structural characteristics of the phase boundaries.
The segregated interfaces will reduce the barrier to dislocation motion and improve slip transmission across phase boundaries.
Improved dislocation transmission across internal interfaces will reduce dislocation pile-ups.
Dislocation transmission or shearing across lamellar interfaces can alleviate local stress concentrations and avoid crack formation.
Lower interfacial stress peaks will delay microcrack initiation.
The segregation treatment will significantly increase room-temperature tensile fracture strain relative to the untreated alloy.
The segregation treatment will maintain or slightly increase yield strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The segregation treatment will maintain or slightly increase ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The proposed effect is applicable under room-temperature quasi-static tensile testing.
The effectiveness of the treatment depends on annealing time, temperature, atmosphere, and the solute species available for segregation.
